opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the picture has gotten a lot clearer over the past year or so. The way I tend to bucket it is into a few categories.

The first, and probably the most mature, is what I'd call knowledge access, or search and retrieval over an enterprise's own data. Every large company has this enormous sprawl of documents, wikis, tickets, emails, contracts, and nobody can find anything. Putting a model on top of that with good retrieval, so an employee can just ask a question and get a grounded answer with citations back to the source, is clearly working. People use it every day, and you can measure the time saved. That's real product-market fit.

The second bucket is customer support and customer-facing assistance. It's a natural fit because the workflows are well defined, there's a lot of historical data on how issues get resolved, and the economics are very legible. If you can deflect a meaningful share of tickets, or make each human agent dramatically more productive by drafting responses and summarizing the case history, the ROI is obvious to a CFO. So that's moved from pilots into production pretty quickly.

The third is what I'd call augmenting knowledge workers in specific verticals: financial analysts, lawyers, people in healthcare administration, sales teams. Summarization, drafting, extracting structured information from messy unstructured documents. It's less about replacing a job and more about removing the drudgery from it, so a person can review ten times as much material or get to a first draft in minutes instead of hours.

And then the fourth, which is the one I'm most excited about but which is earlier on the curve, is agentic workflows, where the model isn't just answering a question but actually taking actions across systems: going into your CRM, your ERP, your ticketing system, and completing a multi-step task end to end. We're seeing real traction there, but it requires a lot more trust, reliability, and integration work, so enterprises are rolling it out more carefully.

The common thread across all of these is that the ones with product-market fit are grounded in the company's own data, sit inside an existing workflow rather than asking people to go somewhere new, and have a clear metric attached. When those three things line up, adoption happens. When they don't, you get a cool demo that never makes it out of the innovation lab.

r001.rationale: It separates broad use cases such as enterprise search and customer support from vertical-specific knowledge-worker assistance, naming finance, law, healthcare administration, and sales.

r002.rationale: It mentions healthcare administration generally, but does not describe passively capturing doctor–patient conversations to populate clinical documentation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about it in a few buckets, and honestly the boundaries are a bit fuzzy, but they're useful.

The first bucket, and the one that's most clearly working, is anything in the retrieval-augmented generation space. Enterprises are sitting on massive amounts of unstructured data: internal documents, support tickets, contracts, research reports, and historically that data was basically dead. Nobody could get at it. So the ability to point a model at that corpus, ground it in the actual documents, and let people ask questions in natural language, that's been the obvious first win. It's knowledge management, it's internal search, it's question answering over your own data. And the key thing that unlocked it was grounding and citations, because that's what made it trustworthy enough for a business to actually deploy.

The second bucket is customer-facing support and service. That's a place where the economics are extremely clear. You've got huge volumes of relatively repetitive interactions, you've got documentation that already exists, and you can measure deflection rates and resolution times very directly. So the ROI story writes itself, and that's why you see so much adoption there.

The third is what I'd broadly call content and document generation. Drafting, summarization, rewriting, pulling structured information out of unstructured text. In banking and insurance, for example, there's just an enormous amount of document processing, and a lot of it is high-volume, low-creativity work that models are very good at. That's less glamorous than people expect, but it's where a lot of the real value is being captured.

And then there's a fourth bucket which is still earlier, which is the more agentic stuff. Models actually taking actions, calling tools, executing multi-step workflows inside the enterprise's systems. We're starting to see real deployments there, but it's harder, because now reliability really matters. When a model just answers a question, a mistake is annoying. When it's updating a CRM or triggering a transaction, a mistake is expensive. So that's where a lot of the work is right now: getting the reliability high enough that enterprises are comfortable handing over actions, not just answers.

I'd also say the things that have product-market fit share some common traits. They're grounded in the enterprise's own data, they have clear metrics attached, and they augment existing workflows rather than asking people to adopt something totally new. The use cases that struggle are the ones that start from "what cool thing can the model do" rather than "what expensive, painful problem does this business actually have."

r001.rationale: The response lists broad use-case buckets and gives banking and insurance as examples, but it does not distinguish industry-specific applications from functions that apply across industries.

r002.rationale: It discusses document processing and generation generally, but does not propose automatically populating clinical documentation from passively captured doctor–patient conversations.

astra-6.text:
I tend to put them into two broad buckets. One is productivity: helping someone do their existing job faster or better. So that might be a coding assistant, or helping someone search internal documents, pull together information, and draft something. The human is still driving, but the model takes a lot of the tedious work off their plate.

The second is automation, where you can hand off a fairly well-defined task. Customer support is an obvious example: there’s a question coming in, there’s information you need to answer it, and there may be an action you need to take. If you can reliably connect those pieces, you can resolve some requests automatically and escalate the others to a person.

The key distinction is how much responsibility you give the model. With an assistant, the person can check its work. With automation, you need a much stronger understanding of where it succeeds, where it fails, and when it should hand control back. So the use cases with the clearest fit tend to be bounded, measurable, and connected to a real workflow.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to put them into three buckets. The first is search and knowledge discovery: helping people find information inside an organization and get an answer grounded in that information. There’s a lot of value in being able to ask a question across your internal documents instead of knowing which document to look for.

The second is assistance—helping someone do their job faster. That might be drafting a response for a customer support agent, helping a developer write code, or helping an analyst summarize material. The human is still driving, but the model takes a lot of the repetitive work off their plate.

And the third is automation: taking a task that previously required someone to read something, make a fairly straightforward decision, and enter information into another system, and having the model do that. Extracting information from documents, categorizing requests, routing them to the right place. Those tasks can sound mundane, but when you’re doing them millions of times, the value is substantial.

r001.rationale: The response gives three broad enterprise use-case buckets but does not distinguish industry-specific applications from functions that apply across industries.
